title: CON Laws
subtitle: Certificate of need · Market entry · State regulation
threatReason: FAH has said nothing on certificate of need in 2025 or 2026. The barrier is falling state by state without it.
fahPosition: No position found. FAH filed no statement, letter, comment or testimony on certificate of need from January 2025 through November 6, 2026. Its May 2025 letter to the FTC and DOJ on anticompetitive regulation does not mention CON.
summary: Certificate of need laws make a new hospital or surgery center ask the state for permission to exist. Incumbents get to object. In 2026, 25 states changed their CON laws and three repealed whole categories. FAH stayed out of it.

status2026.text: Cicero Institute's 2026 ranking: 25 states acted on CON in 2026 sessions. Rhode Island, Iowa and Delaware repealed entire categories. Eight states have no CON law; 42 keep some review.
Rhode Island's FY2027 budget act removed behavioral health, ambulatory surgery centers, home care and CT, MRI and PET imaging from CON. The capital threshold rose to $50 million.

Tennessee Public Chapter 887 ends CON for new acute care hospitals on July 1, 2030, with TennCare and charity care licensure conditions. Satellite emergency departments and cardiac catheterization phase out by 2028.
Iowa HF 2635 repealed CON review for cardiac catheterization, open-heart surgery, organ transplantation, radiation therapy and air ambulance. Cost thresholds rise in steps to $5 million by 2037.
Delaware HB 17 repealed certificate of public review for major medical equipment purchases.
Maine LD 1890 became law without the governor's signature. It exempts most ambulatory surgery centers and raises the capital threshold from $3 million to $7.5 million, indexed to inflation.
The federal lever: CMS's $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program scores CON repeal with Cicero's nine-category method. HFMA counts 17 states that pledged CON reform in their applications.
Entering 2026, Cicero counted 41 states plus DC with some form of CON law.

fahActions.text: FAH's letter to the FTC and DOJ on anticompetitive regulation lists five items. They are noncompetes, 340B eligibility, state mini-HSR acts, the No Surprises Act and the POH ban. Certificate of need is not mentioned.

keyFacts.text: Cicero, October 2026: 25 states acted on CON laws in 2026 and three repealed entire categories of review.
Tennessee's acute care hospital CON ends July 1, 2030, later than the 2028 date in the bill as introduced.
FAH's public comments archive for January 2025 through November 2026 contains no certificate of need letter.

whatItMeans: CON is the state-level wall around incumbent hospitals, and the wall is coming down without FAH's help. The fight is in state capitals, where for-profit chains lobby through state associations, not through FAH. For a physician who wants to build, the live map is the Cicero ranking and the Rural Health Transformation Program scoring, not anything FAH says.

title: Hospital Consolidation
subtitle: FTC authority · Merger review · Noncompetes
threatReason: FAH helped kill the expanded merger form in court and asked the FTC to presume physician noncompetes are fair. The FTC is settling hospital deals, not blocking them.
fahPosition: FAH argues hospital mergers are needed for survival and opposes expanded federal and state premerger reporting. It asks the FTC to treat physician and executive noncompetes as presumptively lawful.
summary: Every merger that closes is one fewer buyer for a physician's services and one more employer that can bind physicians with a noncompete. FAH's 2025 filings pushed on both ends: less merger scrutiny, more noncompete protection. In 2026 it got the merger form vacated, and the FTC has not sued to block a hospital merger in two years.

status2026.text: A federal court in Texas vacated the FTC's 2024 expanded Hart-Scott-Rodino premerger form. AHA and FAH had filed an amicus brief for the plaintiffs in August 2025.
The FTC gave up its noncompete rule, acceding to vacatur and dropping its appeals by a 3 to 1 vote. It says it will pursue noncompetes case by case.
The FTC let Ascension's $3.9 billion purchase of AmSurg close by consent order. Ascension divests seven surgery centers and gives ten years of prior notice in five metros.
FTC consent order: Sevita must divest 128 intermediate care facilities to close its $835 million purchase of BrightSpring's community living business.

Indiana approved the Union Health and Terre Haute Regional merger under a certificate of public advantage over FTC staff and state attorney general objections. FTC staff put the combined share at 74% of commercially insured inpatient care.

No FTC suit to block a hospital-to-hospital merger was found for 2025 or 2026. OhioHealth abandoned its Fairfield Medical Center deal after an FTC investigation; Adena Health then announced it would buy Fairfield.

bills.title: Take Back Our Hospitals Act of 2026 (bars hospitals owned by certain investment firms from Medicare)
bills.sponsor: Sen. Chris Murphy (D-CT) / Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon (D-PA)

fahActions.text: FAH letter to FTC Chairman Ferguson and the DOJ antitrust chief. The noncompete rule distorts competition between nonprofit and taxpaying hospitals. State mini-HSR acts burden mergers. The physician-owned hospital ban must stay.
Joint AHA and FAH amicus brief in Chamber of Commerce v. FTC, arguing mergers are crucial to help hospitals survive and that no problematic hospital merger has evaded review.

FAH comment on the FTC's noncompete inquiry. It asks the agency to presume that senior executives and physicians are fair subjects for noncompetes. It also asks the FTC to defer to 19 state physician-noncompete laws.

keyFacts.text: KFF, 2024 data: 97% of metropolitan areas are highly concentrated for inpatient hospital care under the 2023 merger guidelines. One or two systems controlled the whole inpatient market in 47% of metros.
The August 2025 HSR amicus brief is the only FAH court filing on merger review found for 2025 and 2026.
The joint AHA and FAH brief of July 29, 2024 asked a federal court to vacate the FTC noncompete rule, which covered hospital-employed physicians.

whatItMeans: The two tools that keep an independent physician independent are a competitive local market and the freedom to leave an employer. FAH's 2025 filings worked against both, and the 2026 record shows the FTC settling rather than suing. A physician in a consolidated metro now negotiates with one or two buyers, under a noncompete FAH wants presumed fair.

title: 340B Drug Pricing
subtitle: The 340B program · Contract pharmacy · Medicare payment
threatReason: FAH members are outside the 340B program. FAH backed CMS's cut to acquisition cost and opposes only the recoupment. On this pillar it sits with independent physicians.
fahPosition: FAH says its taxpaying members derive no benefit from 340B discounts. It urged CMS to finalize the 340B payment cut and opposes only the recoupment that offsets the 2018 to 2022 remedy.
summary: The 340B program lets tax-exempt hospitals buy drugs at a discount and bill Medicare and commercial payers at full price. For-profit hospitals cannot join, so FAH has no stake in defending it. In 2026 CMS cut Medicare payment for 340B drugs to acquisition cost minus 28%, with FAH's support.

status2026.text: CMS's CY2027 outpatient final rule pays 340B-acquired drugs at ASP minus 28% from January 1, 2027, based on a 2026 acquisition cost survey. CMS estimates a $4.35 billion cut in Medicare drug payments in year one, redistributed to non-drug services.
The same rule raises the 340B remedy offset on non-drug services from 0.5% to 2% a year, until the $7.8 billion is recovered. CMS now expects that in CY2031.
HRSA approved ten manufacturers covering 21 drugs for round two of the 340B rebate pilot, limited to drugs on the Medicare negotiation lists. Start date January 1, 2027.
AHA, the Maine Hospital Association and four hospitals sued HHS and HRSA in Maine to stop the rebate pilot. They asked for a temporary restraining order. No ruling found as of November 6, 2026.
Round one of the pilot was enjoined in December 2025 and vacated in February 2026 after HHS stopped defending it.
The D.C. Circuit held that HRSA may require the Secretary's approval of any manufacturer rebate model. Manufacturers may not impose rebates on their own.
HRSA: covered entities bought $100 billion of drugs at 340B prices in 2025, up from $81.4 billion in 2024.

bills.title: SUSTAIN 340B Act (sunsets the rebate pilot; codifies contract pharmacy access)
Tax Exempt Hospital Transparency Act (adds 340B, charity care and community benefit reporting to Form 990)
bills.status: Ordered reported by Ways and Means 25 to 15, July 1, 2026

fahActions.text: FAH's letter to the FTC and DOJ lists 340B eligibility rules among the regulations that distort hospital competition.
FAH's CY2026 outpatient comment strongly opposes the retrospective recoupment of $7.8 billion as unlawful.
FAH statement after the Senate HELP 340B hearing: its hospitals derive no benefit from 340B discounts. The program must serve the patients it was meant for.
FAH's CY2027 outpatient comment strongly supports paying 340B drugs at acquisition cost and urges CMS to finalize it. It opposes accelerating the recoupment to 3%.

keyFacts.text: CMS, November 2023: a $9.0 billion lump sum to roughly 1,700 hospitals for 2018 to 2022. A $7.8 billion cut spread over later years offsets it.
HRSA: 2024 purchases at 340B prices were $81.4 billion. Disproportionate share hospitals accounted for $64.1 billion of that.
No FAH position on the HRSA rebate pilot or the contract pharmacy litigation was found.

whatItMeans: The 340B program is the subsidy that lets a tax-exempt system underprice a physician-owned practice on the same infusion. FAH's members do not get it, so FAH pushed CMS to cut it and won. On this one pillar the for-profit lobby and the independent physician want the same thing, for different reasons.

title: No Surprises Act / IDR
subtitle: Independent dispute resolution · QPA · Out-of-network
threatReason: FAH sits with physicians against insurers here. The Fifth Circuit struck the ghost-rate QPA method in August 2026 and the fee fell to $15.
fahPosition: FAH supports the No Surprises Act and blames insurer underpayment for dispute volume. It welcomed the 2026 operations rule. It has joined amicus briefs against the QPA-anchored rules and for enforcement of awards.
summary: The No Surprises Act sent out-of-network pay disputes to arbitration. Insurers built the benchmark, the qualifying payment amount, from contracts that often never covered the service. Physicians have won most disputes anyway. In 2026 the courts and CMS fixed two of the worst mechanics, and FAH cheered both.

status2026.text: The federal IDR operations final rule took effect August 3, 2026. The administrative fee fell from $115 to $15 per party for disputes started on or after June 11, 2026. Plans must disclose QPA information and use standard remittance codes.

The Fifth Circuit, sitting en banc, held the QPA may not include ghost rates for services a contracted physician never furnishes. It may not exclude bonus and incentive payments. Exclusion of single-case agreements was upheld.
The Supreme Court declined to hear Guardian Flight v. HCSC, leaving the Fifth Circuit's holding that the Act gives no private right of action to enforce IDR awards.
Volume: more than 1.46 million federal IDR disputes were started in 2024. Initiating parties won 85% of 2024 determinations and 88% in the first half of 2025.

fahActions.text: FAH's letter to the FTC and DOJ asks the agencies to press insurers to negotiate in good faith and meet IDR requirements. It notes FAH supported the Act at enactment.
FAH statement on IDR costs: insurers are costing Americans billions without improving care, and disputes exist because insurers underpay.
FAH statement on the operations final rule: it adds transparency, accountability and clearer insurer obligations.

keyFacts.text: FAH joined four other hospital groups on a December 2021 brief supporting the AHA and AMA challenge to the IDR interim rule. The others were AAMC, America's Essential Hospitals, the Catholic Health Association and the Children's Hospital Association.
FAH joined AHA, AMA and the Texas Medical Association as amici for the air ambulance appellants in Guardian Flight v. HCSC in October 2024.
The 2021 interim rule assumed 17,333 disputes a year. 2024 brought more than 1.46 million, 84 times the estimate.
CMS: the $15 fee applies to disputes started on or after June 11, 2026; earlier disputes stay at $115.

whatItMeans: This is the one pillar where FAH's interest and the independent physician's line up without a catch. Both bill insurers out of network, both lose when the QPA is rigged, and both win when awards are enforced. The gap that remains is enforcement: a physician who wins arbitration still has no federal right to sue for the money.

title: Physician-Owned Hospital Ban
subtitle: Section 6001 · Stark Law · Repeal bills
threatReason: All four repeal bills are stuck in committee with no hearing. FAH lobbied against one in writing, defended the ban to the FTC, and paid for a study attacking POHs.
fahPosition: FAH urges Congress to maintain current law limiting physician self-referral and calls the ban essential to uphold. It cites conflicts of interest and harm to full-service community hospitals.
summary: Section 6001 of the Affordable Care Act froze physician-owned hospitals in place on March 23, 2010. No new ones can bill Medicare and the old ones cannot add beds. Chip Kahn said the ban would not exist without the Federation. Sixteen years on, FAH is still the guard at the door.

status2026.text: Section 6001 remains in force. No new physician-owned hospital may use the whole-hospital exception, and grandfathered hospitals are frozen at their 2010 bed, operating room and ownership levels. No 119th Congress bill to change it has had a hearing or markup.

FAH and AHA released a Dobson DaVanzo study on sole community hospitals. It claims a new orthopedic POH would cut such a hospital's margin from 2.5% to 1.2%. A cardiac POH would push it to negative 1.2%.
AMA policy and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons back S. 1390 and H.R. 2191. The AMA's August 2025 advocacy update supports lifting the ban.

bills.status: Introduced March 18, 2025; no hearing or markup

bills.status: Introduced April 9, 2025; referred to Finance; no action

bills.status: Introduced June 12, 2025; no hearing or markup

bills.title: Restoring Rights of Physicians to Own Hospitals Act

fahActions.text: FAH's letter to the FTC and DOJ carries a section demanding the POH ban be preserved. It calls the restrictions narrowly tailored and says they prevent cherry-picking.
FAH letter to Reps. Van Duyne and Cuellar opposing H.R. 4002: Congress must maintain current law limiting physician self-referral.
FAH and AHA press release on the sole community hospital study. FAH's policy chief: Congress cannot forget the dangers POHs pose to 24/7 patient care.

keyFacts.text: Chip Kahn, June 1, 2021: the current ban on physician-owned hospitals would not be there without the Federation.
118th Congress: H.R. 977 reached 57 cosponsors and S. 470 reached 14. Neither got a hearing, markup or vote.
No FAH letter or statement on the POH bills has appeared since November 18, 2025.

whatItMeans: This is the pillar FAH exists for. A physician who wants to own the hospital where they operate is barred from Medicare by a 2010 law FAH takes credit for. Four bills would open the door; none has moved. The nine executives on FAH's board run more than 700 hospitals that would face new competition the day the ban falls.

title: Site-Neutral Payments
subtitle: Payment parity · Hospital outpatient vs. physician office · Medicare
threatReason: CMS extended site-neutral rates twice by rule over FAH's written opposition. Site-neutral is the leading pay-for for a year-end package, and FAH is the main obstacle.
fahPosition: FAH opposes every site-neutral expansion. It told CMS in August 2026 that the imaging cut is unlawful and improper and that blunt site-neutral policies ignore hospital cost structures.
summary: Medicare pays a hospital outpatient department more than a physician office for the same visit, scan or infusion. The gap is why hospitals buy practices and why an independent office cannot match a hospital's bid for a physician. CMS has now closed it for drug administration and for imaging. FAH fought both.

status2026.text: CMS's CY2027 outpatient final rule pays imaging without contrast at excepted off-campus hospital departments at the physician fee schedule rate. That is 40% of the hospital rate, from January 1, 2027. CMS estimates $260 million in first-year savings. FAH's comment opposed the cut for 337 imaging services.
The same rule sets a 2.3% outpatient update, removes 637 more services from the inpatient-only list, and raises the 340B remedy offset to 2%.
CMS's CY2026 outpatient final rule paid drug administration at excepted off-campus departments at the physician rate from January 1, 2026, not budget neutral. CMS's estimate was $290 million in 2026.
Executive Order 14273 directed HHS to propose rules so Medicare payment does not steer drug administration to hospital outpatient departments. The CY2026 rule carried it out.
MedPAC repeated in its March and June 2026 reports its recommendation to align payment for 57 ambulatory payment classifications across settings.
HFMA reports site-neutral legislation is seen as the most likely health policy change to pass in 2026, as a pay-for in an end-of-year package. No site-neutral bill was marked up in 2026.

Hospital-side modeling by FTI Consulting for the Coalition to Strengthen America's Healthcare. It says MedPAC's approach would cut hospital payments $182 billion over ten years and nearly $12 billion in year one.

bills.title: Same Care, Lower Cost Act
bills.status: Introduced May 6, 2025; referred to Finance; no action

fahActions.text: FAH's CY2026 outpatient comment opposes site-neutral payment for drug administration at excepted off-campus departments. It calls the cut deeply flawed and unlawful and demands budget neutrality if finalized.
FAH statement on the CY2027 proposed rule objects to accelerated recoupment. Site-neutral is not mentioned by name.

FAH's CY2027 outpatient comment, under the heading Do Not Reduce Payment for Imaging Services at Excepted Off-Campus Departments, calls the cut unlawful and improper. It also opposes removing 637 inpatient-only services.

keyFacts.text: CRFB, Arnold Ventures and West Health estimated $153 billion in lower Medicare spending for 2021 to 2030 from full site-neutral payment.
A Blue Cross Blue Shield Association-commissioned analysis put total savings at $471 billion for 2024 to 2033. That is $231 billion federal, $117 billion in premiums and $152 billion out of pocket.
FAH issue page: blunt site-neutral payment policies ignore fundamental functional and cost structure differences between hospitals and physician offices.
FAH, December 11, 2023, on House passage of H.R. 5378 by 320 to 71: no time for so-called site neutral Medicare cuts.
FAH, November 1, 2024, on the Cassidy-Hassan framework: site-neutral policies threaten access to 24/7 hospital care.

whatItMeans: The site-of-service differential is the single biggest reason a hospital can outbid an independent practice for a physician. Every dollar of parity is a dollar the hospital cannot use to buy the office next door. CMS has moved twice by rule. The congressional version, worth up to $153 billion over ten years, is what FAH's lobbying budget is for.

title: Scope of Practice
subtitle: Nurse practitioners · Physician assistants · State practice acts
threatReason: No FAH statement, comment or letter on scope of practice exists for 2025 or 2026. There is nothing on this pillar to threaten physicians.
fahPosition: No position found. FAH has no documented public position on scope of practice in 2025 or 2026. That covers nurse practitioners, physician assistants, nurse anesthetists, pharmacists and allied health professionals.
summary: Scope of practice is decided in state legislatures, one profession at a time. The for-profit chains that staff emergency rooms and clinics with advanced practice nurses fight those battles through state associations. FAH itself is silent. Its only word on physicians in 2025 was that they are fair subjects for noncompetes.

status2026.text: FAH's public comments archive for January 2025 through November 2026, 49 letters, contains no scope of practice comment. The closest is the November 2025 FTC noncompete letter, which concerns employment, not practice authority.
A fah.org site search for scope of practice returns no relevant item. The results are a 2025 POH study post, a 2024 health IT comment, a 2021 Nurses Week post and a 2019 Ways and Means letter.

keyFacts.text: FAH's November 2025 FTC letter frames physicians only as employees whose noncompetes protect hospital investments. It is the nearest FAH statement on physician practice.

whatItMeans: FAH has no public fight here, which is the finding. The member chains settle scope questions in their own staffing models and through state hospital associations, out of FAH's name. A physician tracking scope bills watches the state capitol and the state hospital association, not Washington.

title: Price Transparency
subtitle: Hospital price files · Shoppable services · Insurer disclosure
threatReason: FAH moved from suing to block disclosure to lobbying for regulatory stability and steering the 2026 bills toward insurers. CMS fined one hospital in 2026 despite 500-plus warnings.
fahPosition: FAH says it supports transparency that gives patients meaningful information. It asks CMS to keep the hospital rules in their current form and tells Congress that patients' costs are dictated primarily by insurers.
summary: FAH sued to stop hospital price disclosure in 2019 and lost twice. In 2025 it asked CMS for regulatory stability. In 2026, with four transparency bills moving through committee, FAH's statements pushed every new duty onto insurers and called added hospital reporting duplicative. The actual-price data an independent practice needs to compete stays patchy.

status2026.text: Executive Order 14221 directed Treasury, Labor and HHS within 90 days to require disclosure of actual prices, not estimates, and to enforce the 2019 order.

CMS's CY2026 outpatient final rule requires machine-readable files to add median, 10th and 90th percentile allowed amounts in dollars. Files must also carry an attestation naming a responsible senior official and the hospital's NPI. Enforcement began April 1, 2026.

The CY2027 proposed rule asked about standardizing machine-readable files and deemed compliance for price estimator tools. The November 4, 2026 final rule fact sheet announces no new hospital price transparency requirement.

CMS's enforcement page lists 28 hospitals fined since 2022: ten in 2025 and one in 2026, Pinnacle Hospital in Indiana. Becker's reports more than 500 hospitals received warning notices or corrective action requests in 2026.

Four bills cleared committee in July 2026: H.R. 9393 (45 to 0) and H.R. 9390 (24 to 21) in Energy and Commerce, H.R. 9645 (25 to 15) in Ways and Means, and S. 2355 (21 to 1) in Senate HELP. They split on whether a price estimator tool satisfies the shoppable services requirement.

fahActions.text: FAH's response to CMS's price transparency inquiry: it does not recommend further regulatory changes at this time. It asks CMS to maintain the hospital rules in their current form.
FAH's CY2026 outpatient comment says it continues to support transparency, but publishing vast amounts of hospital reimbursement data does not help patients.
FAH statement after the House Energy and Commerce transparency hearing: patients' costs are dictated primarily by insurers' benefit design and coverage decisions.
FAH statement on the subcommittee markup: duplicative and impractical hospital reporting requirements will not help patients.
FAH statement on the Ways and Means markup: meaningful transparency requires health plans to provide accurate, real-time information.
FAH statement on the Energy and Commerce full committee markup backs the insurer-side disclosure provisions.
FAH's CY2027 outpatient comment says the current machine-readable file approach does not give patients usable pricing.

keyFacts.text: AHA v. Azar: FAH was a named plaintiff in the December 4, 2019 suit against the hospital price transparency rule. The district court ruled for HHS June 23, 2020; the D.C. Circuit affirmed December 29, 2020.
CMS penalty schedule: $300 a day for hospitals of 30 beds or fewer. Hospitals of 31 to 550 beds pay $10 per bed per day. Above 550 beds it is $5,500 a day.
Of 28 hospitals fined since 2022, one was fined in 2026, for $51,615.

whatItMeans: An independent practice competes on price only if the hospital's price is public and real. FAH lost the lawsuit, then shifted to a quieter strategy: freeze the hospital rules, point at insurers, and call any new hospital duty duplicative. With one fine in 2026, the hospital files stay unreliable, and the price comparison a patient could make stays out of reach.
